description: Under a crust of cooled rock, a fistful of heat going out. To strike, it splits along the seams and flares.
lore: A stretch of the black rock is the wrong colour and warm through the boot, and things get up out of ground argued over that hard. What everyone keeps of a fire is not the flame: it is the black skin that forms over a late log with the red still moving underneath. So that is what stood up — the black rock's ling, a fistful of banked heat in a shell of cooled stone, going out from the moment it got up.

It fights by splitting. The seams open, the flare comes all at once, the shell shuts, and there is a little less inside than there was. You cannot hurry one in any way that is not ugly, so the workers up there walk beside it instead and let it spend itself, and by evening it is down to its last light.

[[characters/cfe826c1|Jehanne]] found one guttering above the tree line on a [[lore/the_age_of_fires|rota]] walk and did what she does at every failing fire on her list: knelt and fed it, stick by stick, half the night, into seams that could not take wood. It went out toward morning anyway. She carries [[items/smouldering_dark_egg|the ember it left]] unsold in her rota coat, and when [[characters/ef25b1f0|Bettany]] asked her, for the Chronicle, why she had fed a thing she knew was not a fire, she gave the answer she gives about the evening prayers: the practice was never for the fire.
